claim: The Mediator complex is a multi-subunit regulator of transcription in eukaryotes that transfers signals from DNA-bound transcription factors to the RNA polymerase II pre-initiation complex.
source: The Mediator complex is a multi-subunit regulator of transcription in eukaryotes that transfers signals from DNA-bound transcription factors to the RNA polymerase II pre-initiation complex (Allen and Taatjes, 2015; Yin and Wang, 2014; Poss et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Allen and Taatjes, 2015; Yin and Wang, 2014; Poss et al., 2013).

claim: The Mediator complex has a role in transcription elongation and pausing.
source: It also has a role in transcription elongation and pausing, and can influence chromatin structure, where it facilitates the formation of enhancer-promoter gene loops and is enriched at 'super-enhancer' regions (Allen and Taatjes, 2015; Poss et al., 2013; Whyte, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Allen and Taatjes, 2015; Poss et al., 2013; Whyte, 2013).

claim: The Mediator complex can influence chromatin structure and facilitates the formation of enhancer-promoter gene loops.
source: It also has a role in transcription elongation and pausing, and can influence chromatin structure, where it facilitates the formation of enhancer-promoter gene loops and is enriched at 'super-enhancer' regions (Allen and Taatjes, 2015; Poss et al., 2013; Whyte, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Allen and Taatjes, 2015; Poss et al., 2013; Whyte, 2013).

claim: The Mediator complex is enriched at 'super-enhancer' regions.
source: It also has a role in transcription elongation and pausing, and can influence chromatin structure, where it facilitates the formation of enhancer-promoter gene loops and is enriched at 'super-enhancer' regions (Allen and Taatjes, 2015; Poss et al., 2013; Whyte, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Allen and Taatjes, 2015; Poss et al., 2013; Whyte, 2013).

claim: Mediator activity is regulated by the association with a four-subunit kinase module containing cyclin-dependent kinase 8 (CDK8), cyclin C (CCNC) and Mediator subunits MED12 and MED13.
source: Mediator activity is regulated by the association with a four-subunit kinase module containing cyclin-dependent kinase 8 (CDK8), cyclin C (CCNC) and Mediator subunits MED12 and MED13 (Allen and Taatjes, 2015; Poss et al., 2013; Taatjes et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Allen and Taatjes, 2015; Poss et al., 2013; Taatjes et al., 2002).

claim: CDK8 is thought to regulate gene expression through phosphorylation of transcription factors and Mediator subunits.
source: As a kinase that reversibly associates with the Mediator, CDK8 is thought to regulate gene expression through phosphorylation of transcription factors and Mediator subunits (Rzymski et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Rzymski et al., 2015).

claim: Phosphorylation by CDK8 can directly alter transcription factor activity.
source: Phosphorylation by CDK8 can directly alter transcription factor activity (Bancerek et al., 2013; Morris et al., 2008; Zhao et al., 2013) or mark factors for degradation (Fryer et al., 2004; Alarcón et al., 2009; Zhao et al., 2012; Li et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Bancerek et al., 2013; Morris et al., 2008; Zhao et al., 2013).

claim: Phosphorylation by CDK8 can mark transcription factors for degradation.
source: Phosphorylation by CDK8 can directly alter transcription factor activity (Bancerek et al., 2013; Morris et al., 2008; Zhao et al., 2013) or mark factors for degradation (Fryer et al., 2004; Alarcón et al., 2009; Zhao et al., 2012; Li et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Fryer et al., 2004; Alarcón et al., 2009; Zhao et al., 2012; Li et al., 2014).

claim: Paralogs of CDK8, MED12 and MED13 have been identified that may have distinct roles in vitro and in vivo.
source: The role of CDK8, and the Mediator kinase module, in the control of transcription may not be unique as paralogs of CDK8, MED12 and MED13 have been identified that may have distinct roles in vitro and in vivo (Sato et al., 2004; Tsutsui et al., 2008; Galbraith et al., 2013; Westerling et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Sato et al., 2004; Tsutsui et al., 2008; Galbraith et al., 2013; Westerling et al., 2007).

claim: The biological function of CDK8 varies by cell type and response to different stimuli.
source: The biological function of CDK8 varies by cell type and response to different stimuli (Allen and Taatjes, 2015; McCleland et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Allen and Taatjes, 2015; McCleland et al., 2015).

claim: CDK8 may function as an oncogene or as a tumor-suppressor depending on the cellular context.
source: This is particularly true in cancer, where CDK8 may function not only as an oncogene, but also as a tumor-suppressor depending on the cellular context (McCleland et al., 2015; Mitra et al., 2006; Chattopadhyay et al., 2010; Gu et al., 2013; Firestein et al., 2008, 2010; Seo et al., 2010; Adler et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (McCleland et al., 2015; Mitra et al., 2006; Chattopadhyay et al., 2010; Gu et al., 2013; Firestein et al., 2008, 2010; Seo et al., 2010; Adler et al., 2012).

claim: CDK8 is amplified in colorectal cancer, with copy number gains observed in ~60% of tumors.
source: CDK8 may act as an oncogene in colorectal cancer where CDK8 is amplified, with copy number gains observed in ~60% of tumors (Firestein et al., 2010; Seo et al., 2010), and shRNA knockdown can reduce the growth of human colorectal cancer xenografts harbouring CDK8 gene amplification (Firestein et al., 2008; Adler et al., 2012; Starr et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Firestein et al., 2010; Seo et al., 2010).

claim: shRNA knockdown of CDK8 can reduce the growth of human colorectal cancer xenografts harbouring CDK8 gene amplification.
source: CDK8 may act as an oncogene in colorectal cancer where CDK8 is amplified, with copy number gains observed in ~60% of tumors (Firestein et al., 2010; Seo et al., 2010), and shRNA knockdown can reduce the growth of human colorectal cancer xenografts harbouring CDK8 gene amplification (Firestein et al., 2008; Adler et al., 2012; Starr et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Firestein et al., 2008; Adler et al., 2012; Starr et al., 2009).

claim: CDK8 expression is reportedly required for growth of colorectal cancer xenografts.
source: Furthermore, CDK8 expression is reportedly required for growth of colorectal cancer xenografts and to maintain embryonic stem cells in an undifferentiated state (Adler et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Adler et al., 2012).

claim: CDK8 expression is required to maintain embryonic stem cells in an undifferentiated state.
source: Furthermore, CDK8 expression is reportedly required for growth of colorectal cancer xenografts and to maintain embryonic stem cells in an undifferentiated state (Adler et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Adler et al., 2012).

claim: CDK8 expression transforms fibroblasts into a malignant phenotype.
source: Importantly, CDK8 expression transforms fibroblasts into a malignant phenotype, whereas expression of a kinase-dead mutant does not (Firestein et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Firestein et al., 2008).

claim: Expression of a kinase-dead CDK8 mutant does not transform fibroblasts into a malignant phenotype.
source: Importantly, CDK8 expression transforms fibroblasts into a malignant phenotype, whereas expression of a kinase-dead mutant does not (Firestein et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Firestein et al., 2008).

claim: An shRNA screen has demonstrated a requirement for CDK8 in the activation of WNT signaling in colorectal cancer.
source: An shRNA screen has also demonstrated a requirement for CDK8 in the activation of WNT signaling in colorectal cancer (Firestein et al., 2008), suggesting that CDK8 and the Mediator kinase module may promote oncogenesis through activation of the canonical WNT pathway.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Firestein et al., 2008).

claim: CDK8 and the Mediator kinase module may promote oncogenesis through activation of the canonical WNT pathway.
source: An shRNA screen has also demonstrated a requirement for CDK8 in the activation of WNT signaling in colorectal cancer (Firestein et al., 2008), suggesting that CDK8 and the Mediator kinase module may promote oncogenesis through activation of the canonical WNT pathway.
evidence: The claim is presented as a suggestion based on inference from the shRNA screen results.

claim: The authors previously reported the discovery and optimization of a potent and selective 3,4,5-trisubstituted pyridine series of small-molecule inhibitors of WNT signaling from a cell-based pathway screen.
source: Previously, we reported the discovery and optimization of a potent and selective 3,4,5-trisubstituted pyridine series of small-molecule inhibitors of WNT signaling from a cell-based pathway screen, and using a chemo-proteomic strategy we identified CDK8 and CDK19 as the primary molecular targets (Dale et al., 2015; Boyer, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to the authors' previous publications (Dale et al., 2015; Boyer, 2015).

claim: Using a chemo-proteomic strategy, CDK8 and CDK19 were identified as the primary molecular targets of the 3,4,5-trisubstituted pyridine series.
source: Previously, we reported the discovery and optimization of a potent and selective 3,4,5-trisubstituted pyridine series of small-molecule inhibitors of WNT signaling from a cell-based pathway screen, and using a chemo-proteomic strategy we identified CDK8 and CDK19 as the primary molecular targets (Dale et al., 2015; Boyer, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to the authors' previous publications (Dale et al., 2015; Boyer, 2015).

claim: Through further optimization, a potent, highly selective and orally bioavailable dual CDK8/19 ligand with excellent cell-based activity and pharmaceutical properties was identified.
source: Through further optimization we identified a potent, highly selective and orally bioavailable dual CDK8/19 ligand with excellent cell-based activity and pharmaceutical properties (Mallinger et al., 2016a).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to the authors' previous publication (Mallinger et al., 2016a).

claim: A second, chemically-distinct series of CDK8/19 ligands was discovered, and optimization identified a 3-methyl-1H-pyrazolo[3,4-b]pyridine that binds to CDK8/CCNC.
source: Subsequently, we discovered a second, chemically-distinct series of CDK8/19 ligands and optimization of pharmacological, pharmaceutical and pharmacokinetic properties identified a 3-methyl-1H-pyrazolo[3,4-b]pyridine, which also binds to CDK8/CCNC (Czodrowski et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to the authors' previous publication (Czodrowski et al., 2016).

claim: Compounds 1 (CCT251545) and 2 (compound 42) fulfill all of the criteria set out for chemical probes.
source: In addition to two tool compounds, 1 (CCT251545; Mallinger et al., 2015) and 2 (compound 42;Mallinger et al., 2016a), that fulfill all of the criteria set out for chemical probes (Frye, 2010), the lead compounds from each of the chemical series, 3 (CCT251921; Mallinger et al., 2016a) and 4 (MSC2530818; Czodrowski et al., 2016) had optimal pharmacological and pharmaceutical properties that made them suitable for further progression to preclinical studies (Figure 1A and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to the authors' previous publications (Mallinger et al., 2015; Mallinger et al., 2016a) and a reference to chemical probe criteria (Frye, 2010).

claim: Compounds 3 (CCT251921) and 4 (MSC2530818) had optimal pharmacological and pharmaceutical properties that made them suitable for further progression to preclinical studies.
source: In addition to two tool compounds, 1 (CCT251545; Mallinger et al., 2015) and 2 (compound 42;Mallinger et al., 2016a), that fulfill all of the criteria set out for chemical probes (Frye, 2010), the lead compounds from each of the chemical series, 3 (CCT251921; Mallinger et al., 2016a) and 4 (MSC2530818; Czodrowski et al., 2016) had optimal pharmacological and pharmaceutical properties that made them suitable for further progression to preclinical studies (Figure 1A and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to the authors' previous publications (Mallinger et al., 2016a; Czodrowski et al., 2016) and reference to Figure 1A and Figure 1—source data 1.

claim: All four compounds (1-4) had single digit nanomolar binding affinities for CDK8 and 19.
source: All four compounds had single digit nanomolar binding affinities for CDK8 and 19, and were very highly selective with little evidence for off-target activity in extended protein kinase panels (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1—source data 1 which contains the experimental data.

claim: All four compounds (1-4) were very highly selective with little evidence for off-target activity in extended protein kinase panels.
source: All four compounds had single digit nanomolar binding affinities for CDK8 and 19, and were very highly selective with little evidence for off-target activity in extended protein kinase panels (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1—source data 1 which contains the experimental data.

claim: The compounds potently inhibited inducible (7dF3) or basal (LS174T) WNT-pathway luciferase-reporter expression at low nanomolar concentrations.
source: Our compounds also potently inhibited inducible (7dF3; Ewan et al., 2010) or basal (LS174T; Dale et al., 2015; Mallinger et al., 2015) WNT-pathway luciferase-reporter expression together with STAT1SER727 phosphorylation ‑ a target-engagement biomarker ‑ at low nanomolar concentrations (Figure 1A and Figure 1—source data 1) (Bancerek et al., 2013; Dale et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Ewan et al., 2010; Dale et al., 2015; Mallinger et al., 2015) and reference to Figure 1A and Figure 1—source data 1.

claim: The compounds potently inhibited STAT1SER727 phosphorylation at low nanomolar concentrations.
source: Our compounds also potently inhibited inducible (7dF3; Ewan et al., 2010) or basal (LS174T; Dale et al., 2015; Mallinger et al., 2015) WNT-pathway luciferase-reporter expression together with STAT1SER727 phosphorylation ‑ a target-engagement biomarker ‑ at low nanomolar concentrations (Figure 1A and Figure 1—source data 1) (Bancerek et al., 2013; Dale et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Bancerek et al., 2013; Dale et al., 2015) and reference to Figure 1A and Figure 1—source data 1.

claim: STAT1SER727 phosphorylation is a target-engagement biomarker for CDK8/19 inhibition.
source: Our compounds also potently inhibited inducible (7dF3; Ewan et al., 2010) or basal (LS174T; Dale et al., 2015; Mallinger et al., 2015) WNT-pathway luciferase-reporter expression together with STAT1SER727 phosphorylation ‑ a target-engagement biomarker ‑ at low nanomolar concentrations (Figure 1A and Figure 1—source data 1) (Bancerek et al., 2013; Dale et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Bancerek et al., 2013; Dale et al., 2015).

claim: Compound 3 binds to CDK8/CCNC in a twisted conformation with the indazole substituent at C5 of the pyridine ring forming a pi-cation interaction with Arg356.
source: Compound 3 binds in a twisted conformation, as previously described for 1, with the indazole substituent at C5 of the pyridine ring forming a pi-cation interaction with Arg356 (Figure 1B) (Mallinger et al., 2015, 2016a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Mallinger et al., 2015, 2016a) and reference to Figure 1B showing the co-crystal structure.

claim: Both compounds 3 and 4 adopt a Type I binding mode and make similar contacts with active site residues of CDK8/CCNC.
source: A comparison of the co-crystal structure of CDK8/CCNC with 3 or 4 showed that both molecules adopt a Type I binding mode and make similar contacts with active site residues (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1B showing the co-crystal structures.

claim: Compound 4 forms similar interactions with the hinge region and with the catalytic Lys52 to those observed for compound 3.
source: Compound 4 forms similar interactions with the hinge region and with the catalytic Lys52 to those observed for compound 3, and its p-chlorophenyl substituent occupies the same region as the indazole subsituent of compound 3; however, the scaffold architecture of the two compounds is entirely different (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1B showing the co-crystal structures.

claim: The scaffold architecture of compounds 3 and 4 is entirely different.
source: Compound 4 forms similar interactions with the hinge region and with the catalytic Lys52 to those observed for compound 3, and its p-chlorophenyl substituent occupies the same region as the indazole subsituent of compound 3; however, the scaffold architecture of the two compounds is entirely different (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1B showing the co-crystal structures.

claim: A strong correlation was observed between the compounds' affinities for both CDK8 and CDK19.
source: Throughout our studies on both chemical series, we observed a strong correlation between the compounds' affinities for both CDK8 and CDK19, suggesting that selective inhibition of CDK8 versus CDK19 is likely to be a significant challenge (Dale et al., 2015; Mallinger et al., 2016a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to the authors' previous publications (Dale et al., 2015; Mallinger et al., 2016a).

claim: Selective inhibition of CDK8 versus CDK19 is likely to be a significant challenge.
source: Throughout our studies on both chemical series, we observed a strong correlation between the compounds' affinities for both CDK8 and CDK19, suggesting that selective inhibition of CDK8 versus CDK19 is likely to be a significant challenge (Dale et al., 2015; Mallinger et al., 2016a).
evidence: The claim is presented as an inference based on the observed correlation between CDK8 and CDK19 affinities.

claim: The strong correlation between CDK8 and CDK19 affinity reflects the high sequence similarity between CDK8 and CDK19.
source: This reflects the high sequence similarity between CDK8 and CDK19 (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1C showing the amino acid sequence alignment.

claim: Selected compounds from three additional chemical series identified from the literature could not detect any substantial selectivity for CDK8 versus CDK19.
source: We also tested selected compounds from a further three chemical series that we identified from the literature and again could not detect any substantial selectivity for CDK8 versus CDK19 (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1—source data 1 which contains the experimental data.

claim: All four compounds potently inhibited a WNT-dependent reporter in all of the colorectal cancer cell lines tested.
source: All four compounds potently inhibited a WNT-dependent reporter in all of the cell lines tested, but did not inhibit a WNT-independent housekeeping EEF1A1 promoter-reporter construct in the negative control RKO colorectal cancer cell line, which expresses low levels of beta-catenin (Figure 1D and Figure 1—source data 1) (Mallinger et al., 2015; Dale et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Mallinger et al., 2015; Dale et al., 2015) and reference to Figure 1D and Figure 1—source data 1.

claim: The compounds did not inhibit a WNT-independent housekeeping EEF1A1 promoter-reporter construct in the negative control RKO colorectal cancer cell line.
source: All four compounds potently inhibited a WNT-dependent reporter in all of the cell lines tested, but did not inhibit a WNT-independent housekeeping EEF1A1 promoter-reporter construct in the negative control RKO colorectal cancer cell line, which expresses low levels of beta-catenin (Figure 1D and Figure 1—source data 1) (Mallinger et al., 2015; Dale et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Mallinger et al., 2015; Dale et al., 2015) and reference to Figure 1D and Figure 1—source data 1.

claim: RKO colorectal cancer cell line expresses low levels of beta-catenin.
source: All four compounds potently inhibited a WNT-dependent reporter in all of the cell lines tested, but did not inhibit a WNT-independent housekeeping EEF1A1 promoter-reporter construct in the negative control RKO colorectal cancer cell line, which expresses low levels of beta-catenin (Figure 1D and Figure 1—source data 1) (Mallinger et al., 2015; Dale et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Mallinger et al., 2015; Dale et al., 2015).

claim: Weakly-active negative-control compounds 5 and 6 did not inhibit reporter gene expression or STAT1SER727 phosphorylation.
source: Weakly-active negative-control compounds from the 3,4,5-trisubstituted pyridine and 3-methyl-1H-pyrazolo[3,4-b]pyridine series (compounds 5 and 6 respectively) did not inhibit reporter gene expression or STAT1SER727 phosphorylation (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1—source data 1 which contains the experimental data.

claim: The potent inhibitors had a lack of effect on tumor cell proliferation after standard 4 d continuous exposure conditions.
source: Given the potent inhibition of reporter activity we were surprised by the lack of effect of our potent inhibitors on tumor cell proliferation after standard 4 d continuous exposure conditions (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1—source data 1 which contains the experimental data.

claim: The lack of antiproliferative effects of CDK8/19 inhibitors was consistent with a reported lack of antiproliferative effects for a different chemical series in a single colorectal cancer cell line.
source: However, this was consistent with a reported lack of antiproliferative effects for a different chemical series in a single colorectal cancer cell line (Koehler et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Koehler et al., 2016).

claim: Silencing of CDK8 and/or CDK19 by shRNA in CDK8-amplified COLO205 cells had no effect on viability, despite evidence for inhibition of reporter output or target gene expression.
source: Silencing of CDK8 and/or CDK19 by shRNA in CDK8-amplified COLO205 cells also had no effect on viability, despite evidence for inhibition of reporter output or target gene expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1A which contains the experimental data.

claim: Knockdown of CDK8 and/or CDK19 by siRNA in CDK8-amplified HT29 cells had no significant effect on viability after 5 d exposure, despite near complete inhibition of STAT1SER727 phosphorylation by the CDK8 siRNA.
source: Knockdown was more effective when we used CDK8 and/or CDK19 siRNA in CDK8-amplified HT29 cells, but again we saw no significant effect on viability after 5 d exposure to siRNA, despite near complete inhibition of STAT1SER727 phosphorylation by the CDK8 siRNA (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C which contains the experimental data.

claim: A 14 d colony growth assay revealed a significantly similar antiproliferative effect for the lead compounds from both chemical series (p<0.001 for all comparisons with 1, 3 and 4).
source: In contrast, a 14 d colony growth assay revealed a significantly similar antiproliferative effect for the lead compounds from both chemical series (p<0.001 for all comparisons with 1, 3 and 4; Figure 1—figure supplement 2), which was not observed for the negative-control compounds 5 and 6.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 2 which contains the experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: The antiproliferative effect in the 14 d colony growth assay was not observed for the negative-control compounds 5 and 6.
source: In contrast, a 14 d colony growth assay revealed a significantly similar antiproliferative effect for the lead compounds from both chemical series (p<0.001 for all comparisons with 1, 3 and 4; Figure 1—figure supplement 2), which was not observed for the negative-control compounds 5 and 6.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 2 which contains the experimental data.

claim: No compounds showed colony growth inhibition in the negative control RKO colorectal cancer cell line.
source: However, no compounds showed colony growth inhibition in the negative control RKO colorectal cancer cell line (Mallinger et al., 2015; Dale et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to the authors' previous publications (Mallinger et al., 2015; Dale et al., 2015).

claim: Three beta-catenin mutant (LS513, LS180, LS174T) and an APC mutant (SW620) colorectal cell lines were most sensitive to treatment in the colony assay.
source: In this assay, we found three beta-catenin mutant (LS513, LS180, LS174T) and an APC mutant (SW620) colorectal cell lines to be most sensitive to treatment (Figure 1E and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1E and Figure 1—source data 1 which contains the experimental data.

claim: The association between beta-catenin mutation and sensitivity to compound treatment in the colony assay did not reach significance (p>0.05).
source: The association between beta-catenin mutation and sensitivity to compound treatment in the colony assay did not reach significance (p>0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by the statistical analysis reported in the text.

claim: Colony growth in RKO cells did not require beta-catenin or CDK8.
source: The lack of response of the RKO cells suggested that colony growth in this line did not require beta-catenin or CDK8 and contrasted with the APC or beta-catenin mutant lines where colony growth appeared to be dependent on beta-catenin-regulated transcription that also required CDK8/19.
evidence: The claim is presented as an inference based on the lack of response of RKO cells to compound treatment.

claim: Colony growth in APC or beta-catenin mutant lines appeared to be dependent on beta-catenin-regulated transcription that also required CDK8/19.
source: The lack of response of the RKO cells suggested that colony growth in this line did not require beta-catenin or CDK8 and contrasted with the APC or beta-catenin mutant lines where colony growth appeared to be dependent on beta-catenin-regulated transcription that also required CDK8/19.
evidence: The claim is presented as an inference based on the differential response of APC or beta-catenin mutant lines compared to RKO cells.

claim: There was no significant correlation between compound activity in TCF-reporter, phospho-biomarker, colony growth assays and either CDK8/19 protein levels or gene copy number.
source: Overall, there was no significant correlation between compound activity in TCF-reporter, phospho-biomarker, colony growth assays and either CDK8/19 protein levels or gene copy number (Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Figure 1—source data 1 which contains the experimental data and correlation analysis.

claim: Compound 1 inhibited TCF/LEF-reporter gene expression and reduced STAT1SER727 phosphorylation by >80% in previous studies.
source: Previously, we demonstrated that compound 1 inhibited TCF/LEF-reporter gene expression and reduced STAT1SER727 phosphorylation by >80%.
evidence: The claim refers to the authors' previous work.

claim: Compound 1 reduced tumor growth following oral dosing in mice bearing established COLO205 or SW620 colorectal cancer cell xenografts.
source: This translated into tumor growth inhibition following oral dosing of 1 in mice bearing established COLO205 or SW620 colorectal cancer cell xenografts (Mallinger et al., 2015; Dale et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to the authors' previous publications (Mallinger et al., 2015; Dale et al., 2015).

claim: There was evidence for a significant, dose-dependent, reduction in tumor growth in HCT116 human colorectal cancer cell line xenografts treated with compound 1.
source: We also found evidence for a significant, dose-dependent, reduction in tumor growth in HCT116 human colorectal cancer cell line xenografts as well as significant tumor growth inhibition (TGI = 81%; p<0.001) at 70 mg/kg in an LS513 human colorectal cancer xenograft model with concomitant reduction of p-STAT1SER727 at 6 hr (Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 2—source data 1 which contains the experimental data.

claim: Compound 1 showed significant tumor growth inhibition (TGI = 81%; p<0.001) at 70 mg/kg in an LS513 human colorectal cancer xenograft model with concomitant reduction of p-STAT1SER727 at 6 hr.
source: We also found evidence for a significant, dose-dependent, reduction in tumor growth in HCT116 human colorectal cancer cell line xenografts as well as significant tumor growth inhibition (TGI = 81%; p<0.001) at 70 mg/kg in an LS513 human colorectal cancer xenograft model with concomitant reduction of p-STAT1SER727 at 6 hr (Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 2—source data 1 which contains the experimental data.

claim: Maximal inhibition of STAT1SER727 phosphorylation in HCT116 tumor xenografts required treatment with ≥5 mg/kg compound 3.
source: Detailed analysis, initially in HCT116 tumor xenografts, showed that maximal inhibition of STAT1SER727 phosphorylation required treatment with ≥5 mg/kg compound 3 and that higher concentrations prolonged the period of maximal inhibition (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–C which contains the experimental data.

claim: Higher concentrations of compound 3 prolonged the period of maximal inhibition of STAT1SER727 phosphorylation in HCT116 tumor xenografts.
source: Detailed analysis, initially in HCT116 tumor xenografts, showed that maximal inhibition of STAT1SER727 phosphorylation required treatment with ≥5 mg/kg compound 3 and that higher concentrations prolonged the period of maximal inhibition (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–C which contains the experimental data.

claim: In SW620 tumor xenografts, biomarker inhibition was rapidly achieved following treatment with 3 or 4.
source: In SW620 tumor xenografts biomarker inhibition was rapidly achieved following treatment with 3 or 4 and could be maintained for approximately 10 hr after a single treatment with 30 mg/kg of 3, while 30 or 100 mg/kg of 4 prolonged the period of inhibition of STAT1SER727 phosphorylation so that, unlike 3, multiple dosing with 4 prevented recovery of biomarker to control levels between treatments (Figures 2A,3D–E, Figure 2—figure supplement 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figures 2A, 3D–E, Figure 2—figure supplement 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 3B which contain the experimental data.

claim: Biomarker inhibition could be maintained for approximately 10 hr after a single treatment with 30 mg/kg of compound 3 in SW620 tumor xenografts.
source: In SW620 tumor xenografts biomarker inhibition was rapidly achieved following treatment with 3 or 4 and could be maintained for approximately 10 hr after a single treatment with 30 mg/kg of 3, while 30 or 100 mg/kg of 4 prolonged the period of inhibition of STAT1SER727 phosphorylation so that, unlike 3, multiple dosing with 4 prevented recovery of biomarker to control levels between treatments (Figures 2A,3D–E, Figure 2—figure supplement 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figures 2A, 3D–E, Figure 2—figure supplement 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 3B which contain the experimental data.

claim: 30 or 100 mg/kg of compound 4 prolonged the period of inhibition of STAT1SER727 phosphorylation in SW620 tumor xenografts so that multiple dosing prevented recovery of biomarker to control levels between treatments.
source: In SW620 tumor xenografts biomarker inhibition was rapidly achieved following treatment with 3 or 4 and could be maintained for approximately 10 hr after a single treatment with 30 mg/kg of 3, while 30 or 100 mg/kg of 4 prolonged the period of inhibition of STAT1SER727 phosphorylation so that, unlike 3, multiple dosing with 4 prevented recovery of biomarker to control levels between treatments (Figures 2A,3D–E, Figure 2—figure supplement 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figures 2A, 3D–E, Figure 2—figure supplement 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 3B which contain the experimental data.

claim: Both lead compounds 3 and 4 exhibited reproducible, dose-dependent antitumor activity in SW620 tumor xenografts.
source: Both lead compounds 3 and 4 exhibited reproducible, dose-dependent antitumor activity in SW620 tumor xenografts (Figure 2D–E, Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–B and Figure 2—source data 1) and also in an additional LS1034 colorectal tumor model that responded to our compounds in the in vitro clonogenic assay (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C–E, Figure 2—figure supplement 4 and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2D–E, Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–B and Figure 2—source data 1 which contain the experimental data.

claim: Compounds 3 and 4 showed antitumor activity in an LS1034 colorectal tumor model that responded to the compounds in the in vitro clonogenic assay.
source: Both lead compounds 3 and 4 exhibited reproducible, dose-dependent antitumor activity in SW620 tumor xenografts (Figure 2D–E, Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–B and Figure 2—source data 1) and also in an additional LS1034 colorectal tumor model that responded to our compounds in the in vitro clonogenic assay (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C–E, Figure 2—figure supplement 4 and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 3C–E, Figure 2—figure supplement 4 and Figure 2—source data 1 which contain the experimental data.

claim: 5 mg/kg compound 3 induced maximal inhibition of STAT1SER727 phosphorylation in SW620 human tumor xenografts, but its effects were short-lived and were not sufficient to translate into antitumor activity.
source: While 5 mg/kg compound 3 induced maximal inhibition of STAT1SER727 phosphorylation in SW620 human tumor xenografts, its effects were short-lived, and were not sufficient to translate into antitumor activity (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 2D and Figure 2—source data 1 which contain the experimental data.

claim: Higher 30 mg/kg doses of compound 3 prolonged the maximal inhibition of STAT1SER727 phosphorylation and had a significant (p<0.01) antitumor effect.
source: However, higher 30 mg/kg doses of compound 3 prolonged the maximal inhibition of STAT1SER727 phosphorylation and had a significant (p<0.01) antitumor effect (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–B and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–B and Figure 2—source data 1 which contain the experimental data.

claim: 10 mg/kg of compound 4 inhibited the pathway biomarker for 6 hr, but was not sufficient for antitumor activity in SW620 xenografts.
source: As with 3, 10 mg/kg of 4 inhibited the pathway biomarker for 6 hr, but was not sufficient for antitumor activity in SW620 xenografts (Figure 2A and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2A and Figure 2—source data 1 which contain the experimental data.

claim: Repeated dosing of compound 4 at 50 or 100 mg/kg prolonged the inhibition of STAT1SER727 phosphorylation and gave evidence of antitumor activity.
source: However, repeated dosing of 4 at 50 or 100 mg/kg prolonged the inhibition of STAT1SER727 phosphorylation and gave evidence of antitumor activity (Figure 2D–E and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2D–E and Figure 2—source data 1 which contain the experimental data.

claim: The antitumor activity of compounds 3 and 4 against colorectal cancer xenografts showed clear dose-dependence, with a requirement for prolonged pathway inhibition in order to significantly reduce tumor growth.
source: Hence, the antitumor activity of 3 and 4 against colorectal cancer xenografts showed clear dose-dependence, with a requirement for prolonged pathway inhibition in order to significantly reduce tumor growth.
evidence: The claim is presented as a conclusion based on the experimental data showing dose-dependent effects and the relationship between pathway inhibition duration and antitumor activity.

claim: Colony growth was inhibited, but only by up to 50%, in one-third of PDX cell cultures treated with tool compound 2 in soft agar clonogenic assays.
source: Firstly, we determined if our compounds were active in in vitro soft agar clonogenic assays, using cells derived from 89 distinct PDX models from different tissue types. In this assay, colony growth was inhibited, but only by up to 50%, in one-third of PDX cell cultures treated with tool compound 2 (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 3A–B which contains the experimental data.

claim: Only two of six colorectal cancer PDX tumor models (CFX 883 and CFX 1753) responded to monotherapy with compound 3 (p<0.0001).
source: Only two of these colorectal cancer PDX tumors models, CFX 883 and CFX 1753, responded to monotherapy with 3 (p<0.0001; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 1A which contains the experimental data.

claim: The combination of compound 3 with standard of care therapies was only of statistically significant benefit in one colorectal tumor model, CFX 1034 (p<0.001).
source: Importantly, the combination of 3 with standard of care therapies was only of statistically significant benefit in one colorectal tumor model, CFX 1034 (p<0.001; Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1 which contain the experimental data.

claim: Examination of p-STAT1SER727 levels indicated near maximal CDK8 inhibition in three PDX tumors tested (p<0.0001).
source: Examination of p-STAT1SER727 levels indicated near maximal CDK8 inhibition in the three tumors where p-STAT1SER727 was tested (p<0.0001; Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and D), indicating that the failure of 3 to slow PDX growth (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and F) was unlikely to be due to a lack of target engagement.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and D which contain the experimental data.

claim: The failure of compound 3 to slow PDX growth was unlikely to be due to a lack of target engagement.
source: Examination of p-STAT1SER727 levels indicated near maximal CDK8 inhibition in the three tumors where p-STAT1SER727 was tested (p<0.0001; Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and D), indicating that the failure of 3 to slow PDX growth (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and F) was unlikely to be due to a lack of target engagement.
evidence: The claim is presented as an inference based on the observation of near maximal CDK8 inhibition despite lack of tumor growth inhibition.

claim: The Nomo-1 AML cell line was particularly sensitive to treatment with compound 2 with an 11 nM GI50.
source: The most CDK8/19 inhibitor sensitive cell model in the soft agar assays was one of the two acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) cell lines, Nomo-1, included in the cell panel. The Nomo-1 line was particularly sensitive to treatment with compound 2 (Figure 3A) with an 11 nM GI50.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 3A which contains the experimental data.

claim: Treatment with compound 3 led to a potent reduction in circulating tumor cells in a Nomo-1 systemic in vivo model.
source: Subsequently, in a Nomo-1 systemic in vivo model, treatment with 3 led to a potent reduction in circulating tumor cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–B which contains the experimental data.

claim: A subcutaneous MV-4-11 AML xenograft responded to monotherapy (TGI = 100%) with 10 mg/kg po qd compound 3.
source: An additional subcutaneous MV-4-11 AML xenograft also responded to monotherapy (TGI = 100%) with 10 mg/kg po qd 3, and also with 4 which showed evidence of near maximal target inhibition, as determined using p-STAT1SER727 at 2 hr post-treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 2C–D which contains the experimental data.

claim: MV-4-11 AML xenograft responded to compound 4 which showed evidence of near maximal target inhibition, as determined using p-STAT1SER727 at 2 hr post-treatment.
source: An additional subcutaneous MV-4-11 AML xenograft also responded to monotherapy (TGI = 100%) with 10 mg/kg po qd 3, and also with 4 which showed evidence of near maximal target inhibition, as determined using p-STAT1SER727 at 2 hr post-treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 2C–D which contains the experimental data.

claim: 278 transcription factor-associated genesets were enriched in genes whose expression was significantly altered following in vivo treatment of COLO205 or SW620 human tumor xenografts.
source: We initially identified 278 transcription factor-associated genesets that were enriched in genes whose expression was significantly altered following in vivo treatment of COLO205 or SW620 human tumor xenografts.
evidence: The claim is supported by the gene expression microarray profiling analysis described in the text.

claim: 121 out of 278 transcription factor-associated genesets were identified following treatment of both COLO205 and SW620 xenografts.
source: The altered expression of 121/278 of these transcription factor-associated genesets was identified following treatment of both xenografts (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 4A which contains the experimental data.

claim: 185 transcription factor-associated genesets were significantly enriched in sets of genes associated with super-enhancers.
source: Of note we also identified 185 transcription factor-associated genesets that were significantly enriched in sets of genes associated with super-enhancers; of these, 2/3rds were shared with the genesets whose expression was altered by compound treatment (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 4A which contains the experimental data.

claim: 2/3rds of the 185 transcription factor-associated genesets enriched in super-enhancer genes were shared with the genesets whose expression was altered by compound treatment.
source: Of note we also identified 185 transcription factor-associated genesets that were significantly enriched in sets of genes associated with super-enhancers; of these, 2/3rds were shared with the genesets whose expression was altered by compound treatment (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 4A which contains the experimental data.

claim: Common transcription factor genesets included transcription factors known to be regulated by CDK8, such as TCF4, SMADs, STATs, c/EBP and HIF1A.
source: These common transcription factor genesets included transcription factors known to be regulated by CDK8, such as TCF4, SMADs, STATs, c/EBP and HIF1A (Figure 4—source data 1) (Bancerek et al., 2013; Morris et al., 2008; Zhao et al., 2013; Fryer et al., 2004; Alarcón et al., 2009; Zhao et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Bancerek et al., 2013; Morris et al., 2008; Zhao et al., 2013; Fryer et al., 2004; Alarcón et al., 2009; Zhao et al., 2012) and reference to Figure 4—source data 1.

claim: The genesets shared between both treatment and super-enhancers encompassed transcription factors (NANOG, OCT3/4 and SOX2) required for stem cell pluripotency.
source: The genesets shared between both treatment and super-enhancers also encompassed transcription factors (NANOG, OCT3/4 and SOX2) required for stem cell pluripotency (Figure 4—source data 1) (Whyte et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Whyte et al., 2013) and reference to Figure 4—source data 1.

claim: 85 genesets encoding specific pathway components were significantly enriched in the pool of genes whose expression was modulated by compound treatment.
source: A similar analysis, but this time of genes encoding specific pathway components, found 85 genesets were significantly enriched in the pool of genes whose expression was modulated by compound treatment (Figure 4A); 15 of which were found in both colorectal cancer xenograft experiments.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 4A which contains the experimental data.

claim: 15 out of 85 pathway-associated genesets were found in both COLO205 and SW620 colorectal cancer xenograft experiments.
source: A similar analysis, but this time of genes encoding specific pathway components, found 85 genesets were significantly enriched in the pool of genes whose expression was modulated by compound treatment (Figure 4A); 15 of which were found in both colorectal cancer xenograft experiments.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 4A which contains the experimental data.

claim: A third of the 15 common pathway-associated genesets were associated with WNT signaling.
source: A third of these were geneset-encoded gene products associated with WNT signaling, while others encoded components of individual pathways involved in development, inflammation or osteoblast biology (Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 4—source data 1 which contains the experimental data.

claim: Five of the genesets common to both tumor models, all comprising WNT pathway components, were enriched with super-enhancer associated genes.
source: Five of the genesets, common to both tumor models, all comprising WNT pathway components, were enriched with super-enhancer associated genes.
evidence: The claim is supported by the gene expression analysis described in the text.

claim: Treatment of both tumor models resulted in a consistent and significant modulation of genes in the vicinity of MED1 and CDK8-associated super-enhancers identified from ChIP-seq datasets.
source: We found that treatment of both tumor models resulted in a consistent and significant modulation of genes in the vicinity of MED1 and CDK8-associated super-enhancers identified from ChIP-seq datasets (Figure 4B–C and Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 4B–C and Figure 4—source data 1 which contain the experimental data.

claim: Super-enhancers defined by a BRD4 ChIP-seq in lymphoid cells did not show the same significant modulation as the MED1/CDK8-defined super-enhancers.
source: Interestingly, super-enhancers defined by a BRD4 ChIP-seq in lymphoid cells did not show the same significant modulation as the MED1/CDK8-defined super-enhancers (Figure 4B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 4B–C which contains the experimental data.

claim: The expression of many MSigDB genesets were positively or negatively correlated with the compound-treated samples and included genesets encoding gene products associated with, or regulated by, developmental, immunological or inflammatory pathways.
source: The expression of many of the MSigDB genesets were positively or negatively correlated with the compound-treated samples and included genesets encoding gene products associated with, or regulated by, developmental, immunological or inflammatory pathways (Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 4—source data 1 which contains the experimental data.

claim: Genesets with decreased expression associated with stem cell pluripotency (SOX2, NANOG and OCT4) were modulated by treatment in both tumor models and with both compounds 1 and 3.
source: Some patterns were common to all treated samples, for example the genesets with decreased expression associated with stem cell pluripotency (SOX2, NANOG and OCT4) were modulated by treatment in both of the tumor models and also with both 1 and 3 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1 which contains the experimental data.

claim: The expression of bone morphogenic protein 2 (BMP2)-regulated genes and others associated with bone remodelling were inhibited by treatment of COLO205 xenografts, but were activated in SW620 xenografts.
source: In contrast, other genesets exhibited cell line-specific regulation, for example the expression of bone morphogenic protein 2 (BMP2)-regulated genes and others associated with bone remodelling were inhibited by treatment of COLO205 xenografts, but were activated in SW620 xenografts (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1 which contains the experimental data.

claim: The altered levels of transcripts from genes influenced by transcription factors or super-enhancers known to be regulated by the Mediator complex and CDK8 are consistent with the compounds affecting a broad range of CDK8/19-regulated gene transcription.
source: Overall, the altered levels of transcripts from genes influenced by transcription factors or super-enhancers known to be regulated by the Mediator complex and CDK8 are consistent with our compounds affecting a broad range of CDK8/19-regulated gene transcription (Mallinger et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is presented as a conclusion based on the gene expression profiling data and is supported by a citation to the authors' previous publication (Mallinger et al., 2015).

claim: The genes and genesets identified suggested that effects on stem cells, bone, immunology and inflammation might influence compound tolerability.
source: The genes and genesets identified suggested that effects on stem cells, bone, immunology and inflammation might influence compound tolerability (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is presented as a speculation based on the gene expression profiling data.

claim: High-level induction of beta-catenin with 2 mg/mL Dox significantly increased the percentage of stem cells (GRP78−) in the crypt cell compartment.
source: High-level induction of beta-catenin with 2 mg/mL Dox significantly increased the percentage of stem cells (GRP78−) in the crypt cell compartment, whereas lower-level induction with 0.1 mg/mL Dox was associated with a larger transit amplifying (GRP78+) cell population, as previously described (Figure 5B–C) (Hirata et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Hirata et al., 2013) and reference to Figure 5B–C which contains the experimental data.

claim: Lower-level induction with 0.1 mg/mL Dox was associated with a larger transit amplifying (GRP78+) cell population.
source: High-level induction of beta-catenin with 2 mg/mL Dox significantly increased the percentage of stem cells (GRP78−) in the crypt cell compartment, whereas lower-level induction with 0.1 mg/mL Dox was associated with a larger transit amplifying (GRP78+) cell population, as previously described (Figure 5B–C) (Hirata et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Hirata et al., 2013) and reference to Figure 5B–C which contains the experimental data.

claim: Complete withdrawal of Dox inhibited WNT signaling in the stem cell population, confirmed by a change in the abundance of transcripts from the WNT-regulated genes Axin2 and Car4.
source: The complete withdrawal of Dox inhibited WNT signaling in the stem cell population, confirmed by a change in the abundance of transcripts from the WNT-regulated genes Axin2 and Car4 (Figure 5D–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 5D–E which contains the experimental data.

claim: Dox withdrawal did not significantly alter the ratio of stem to TA cells.
source: However, Dox withdrawal did not significantly alter the ratio of stem to TA cells (Figure 5B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 5B–C which contains the experimental data.

claim: Reducing the degree of Dox-induction from 2 to 0.1 mg/ml shifted the population towards an increased proportion of TA cells.
source: In contrast, reducing the degree of Dox-induction from 2 to 0.1 mg/ml shifted the population towards an increased proportion of TA cells (Figure 5B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 5B–C which contains the experimental data.

claim: Treatment with compound 1 at 75 mg/kg x 3 over 24 hr resulted in a gene expression pattern in the stem cell fraction that was similar to both Dox-removal and reduction of Dox from 2.0 to 0.1 mg/ml.
source: Here, we found that treatment with 1 at 75 mg/kg x 3 over 24 hr resulted in a gene expression pattern in the stem cell fraction that was similar to both Dox-removal and reduction of Dox from 2.0 to 0.1 mg/ml (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 5D which contains the experimental data.

claim: The gene expression in the TA fraction following treatment with compound 1 was similar to the effect of reducing the level of Dox from 2.0 to 0.1 mg/ml, but was different from the Dox withdrawal condition.
source: In contrast, the gene expression in the TA fraction following treatment with 1 was similar to the effect of reducing the level of Dox from 2.0 to 0.1 mg/ml, but was different from the Dox withdrawal condition (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 5E which contains the experimental data.

claim: Treatment with compound 1 resulted in a shift in the population distribution from stem cell to TA similar to that seen by reducing the level of Dox from 2.0 to 0.1 mg/ml.
source: This observation was consistent with the observation that treatment with 1 resulted in a shift in the population distribution from stem cell to TA similar to that seen by reducing the level of Dox from 2.0 to 0.1 mg/ml (Figure 5B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 5B–C which contains the experimental data.

claim: The inhibition of CDK8/19 by compound 1 reduces, rather than eliminates, WNT signaling in the oncogenically-activated stem cell compartment and it is this that alters the proportion of stem cells to proliferative TA cells in the hyperplastic crypt.
source: This implies that the inhibition of CDK8/19 by 1 reduces, rather than eliminates, WNT signaling in the oncogenically-activated stem cell compartment and it is this that alters the proportion of stem cells to proliferative TA cells in the hyperplastic crypt.
evidence: The claim is presented as an inference based on the experimental observations of gene expression and cell population shifts.

claim: Treatment with LGK974, a Porcupine inhibitor that inhibits WNT signaling, reduced secretion of Procollagen type I N-terminal propeptide (PINP) in mouse KS483 osteoprogenitor cells.
source: We treated mouse KS483 osteoprogenitor cells with LGK974, a Porcupine inhibitor that inhibits WNT signaling, and observed reduced secretion of Procollagen type I N-terminal propeptide (PINP), an organic component of bone, and also reduced deposition of calcium, an inorganic component of bone (Figure 6A–B) (Dang et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Dang et al., 2002) and reference to Figure 6A–B which contains the experimental data.

claim: Treatment with LGK974 reduced deposition of calcium in mouse KS483 osteoprogenitor cells.
source: We treated mouse KS483 osteoprogenitor cells with LGK974, a Porcupine inhibitor that inhibits WNT signaling, and observed reduced secretion of Procollagen type I N-terminal propeptide (PINP), an organic component of bone, and also reduced deposition of calcium, an inorganic component of bone (Figure 6A–B) (Dang et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Dang et al., 2002) and reference to Figure 6A–B which contains the experimental data.

claim: Compound 3 stimulated PINP secretion at low concentrations and inhibited PINP secretion at higher concentrations in mouse KS483 osteoprogenitor cells.
source: In contrast, compound 3 stimulated PINP secretion at low concentrations and inhibited PINP secretion at higher concentrations (Figure 6A), while calcium deposition was inhibited in a concentration-dependent manner (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 6A which contains the experimental data.

claim: Compound 3 inhibited calcium deposition in a concentration-dependent manner in mouse KS483 osteoprogenitor cells.
source: In contrast, compound 3 stimulated PINP secretion at low concentrations and inhibited PINP secretion at higher concentrations (Figure 6A), while calcium deposition was inhibited in a concentration-dependent manner (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 6B which contains the experimental data.

claim: Compound 3 adversely affects bone development in an in vitro model and its effects are distinct from a specific inhibitor of WNT signaling.
source: These data indicate that our lead compound 3 adversely affects bone development in an in vitro model and that its effects are distinct from a specific inhibitor of WNT signaling.
evidence: The claim is presented as a conclusion based on the experimental data comparing compound 3 to LGK974.

claim: All four compounds (1–4) elicited a similar biomarker response across the cell line panel (median r = 0.812; range: 0.630 – 0.924).
source: All four compounds (1–4) elicited a similar biomarker response across the cell line panel (median r = 0.812; range: 0.630 – 0.924), indicating that the observed changes were the result of CDK8/19 inhibition rather than off-target effects.
evidence: The claim is supported by the correlation analysis of biomarker responses.

claim: The observed biomarker changes in co-culture models were the result of CDK8/19 inhibition rather than off-target effects.
source: All four compounds (1–4) elicited a similar biomarker response across the cell line panel (median r = 0.812; range: 0.630 – 0.924), indicating that the observed changes were the result of CDK8/19 inhibition rather than off-target effects.
evidence: The claim is presented as an inference based on the similar biomarker responses across all four compounds.

claim: Comparing the effects of the compounds with a proprietary database of >3000 approved drugs and experimental agents failed to find any close matches.
source: Comparing the effects of our compounds with a proprietary database of >3000 approved drugs and experimental agents failed to find any close matches (Berg et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Berg et al., 2010).

claim: Treatment with the compounds elicited an unusual split response, with an increase in IL-17A and a corresponding decrease in IL-17F.
source: The levels of interleukin 17A and 17F usually rise and fall together (Melton et al., 2013), but treatment with our compounds elicited an unusual split response, with an increase in IL-17A and a corresponding decrease in IL-17F (BT condition: Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Melton et al., 2013) and reference to Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and Figure 6—source data 1 which contain the experimental data.

claim: The pattern observed across the biomarkers was consistent with the effects of the compounds on inflammation (VCAM-1, sPGE2 and IL-8), immunomodulation (IL-17A, IL-17F, HLA-DR and IgG) and tissue remodelling (uPAR).
source: Overall, the pattern observed across the biomarkers was consistent with the effects of our compounds on inflammation (VCAM-1, sPGE2 and IL-8), immunomodulation (IL-17A, IL-17F, HLA-DR and IgG) and tissue remodelling (uPAR) (Figure 6C and Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 6C and Figure 6—source data 1 which contain the experimental data.

claim: In rats treated with compound 3, only IL-12, a proinflammatory and proimmunestimulatory cytokine, increased significantly (p<0.005) out of ten plasma cytokines measured.
source: In additional studies in rats treated with 3 we measured the levels of ten plasma cytokines associated with the Th1/Th2 immune response. Of the cytokines measured, only IL-12, a proinflammatory and proimmunestimulatory cytokine, increased significantly (p<0.005, Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 6D which contains the experimental data.

claim: Compounds from both chemical series were sufficiently well tolerated in mice to enable antitumor experiments to be conducted with a dosage regimen that resulted in near-maximal inhibition of tumor STAT1SER727 phosphorylation.
source: Compounds from both chemical series were sufficiently well tolerated in mice to enable antitumor experiments to be conducted with a dosage regimen that resulted in near-maximal inhibition of tumor STAT1SER727 phosphorylation, showing that CDK8/19 activity was repressed for prolonged periods (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplements 1–3, Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to multiple figures which contain the experimental data.

claim: There was some evidence for body weight loss in mice that sometimes necessitated short dosing breaks.
source: However, there was some evidence for body weight loss that sometimes necessitated short dosing breaks (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2—source data 1 which contains the experimental data.

claim: Following daily doses of compound 3 or 4 for 14 days in rats, significant, adverse alterations in multiple organ systems and tissues were detected.
source: Following daily doses of compound 3 or 4 for 14 days in rats we detected significant, adverse alterations in multiple organ systems and tissues (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Table 1 which contains the experimental data.

claim: Extensive (80%) inhibition of STAT1SER727 phosphorylation was demonstrated 6 hr post-treatment at all doses of compound 3 tested in rat toleration studies.
source: In these toleration studies, we demonstrated extensive (80%) inhibition of STAT1SER727 phosphorylation 6 hr post-treatment at all doses of 3 tested (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 7—figure supplement 1 which contains the experimental data.

claim: The lowest doses of compounds 3 and 4 administered in rat studies resulted in plasma concentrations below or equivalent to the plasma exposures achieved at efficacious doses in experimental human tumor xenograft efficacy models, suggesting the lack of a clear therapeutic window.
source: The lowest doses administered resulted in plasma concentrations below or equivalent to the plasma exposures achieved at efficacious doses in our experimental human tumor xenograft efficacy models, suggesting the lack of a clear therapeutic window (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is presented as an inference based on the comparison of plasma exposures and is supported by reference to Table 1.

claim: The rat studies revealed two different, paradoxical effects on bone: an inhibitory effect resulting in dysplasia of the growth plate, a decrease in the proliferative zone and false endochondral ossification, and an activating effect resulting in proliferation of irregular woven bone in the bone cavity and below the periosteum.
source: Consistent with our in vitro observations of the effects on bone maturation, the rat studies revealed two different, paradoxical effects on bone: an inhibitory effect resulting in dysplasia of the growth plate, a decrease in the proliferative zone and false endochondral ossification, and an activating effect resulting in proliferation of irregular woven bone in the bone cavity and below the periosteum (Table 1 and Figure 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Table 1 and Figure 7 which contain the experimental data.

claim: Other adverse pathomorphological findings in rats included necrotic and apoptotic cell lesions in the exocrine pancreas, gastrointestinal mucosa (stomach and duodenum), male reproductive tract, mammary gland, skin (hair follicle), heart (valvular interstitial cells) and lymphatic tissues (thymus, spleen, lymph nodes).
source: Other adverse pathomorphological findings included necrotic and apoptotic cell lesions in the exocrine pancreas, gastrointestinal mucosa (stomach and duodenum), male reproductive tract (Figure 7), mammary gland, skin (hair follicle), heart (valvular interstitial cells) and lymphatic tissues (thymus, spleen, lymph nodes).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 7 which contains the experimental data.

claim: Proliferative lesions in rats were found in the lungs (bronchiolar epithelium and smooth muscle cells), liver (bile ducts and smooth muscle cells of hepatic arteries), thymus (epithelium free areas), mammary gland, male reproductive system and heart (valvular interstitial cells).
source: Proliferative lesions were found in the lungs (bronchiolar epithelium and smooth muscle cells), liver (bile ducts and smooth muscle cells of hepatic arteries), thymus (epithelium free areas), mammary gland, male reproductive system and heart (valvular interstitial cells) (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Table 1 which contains the experimental data.

claim: Follow-up studies in dogs indicated a similar, widespread adverse safety profile at therapeutically relevant exposures of compounds 3 and 4.
source: Follow-up studies in dogs indicated a similar, widespread adverse safety profile at therapeutically relevant exposures of 3 and 4 (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Table 1 which contains the experimental data.

claim: The adverse effects of treatment with compounds 3 and 4 are the direct result of inhibition of CDK8 and/or CDK19.
source: Since these pathological effects were seen with two highly selective, but structurally distinct CDK8/19 inhibitors in both rats and dogs, we conclude that the adverse effects of treatment are the direct result of inhibition of CDK8 and/or CDK19.
evidence: The claim is presented as a conclusion based on the observation of similar adverse effects with two structurally distinct inhibitors in two species.

claim: The clinical development of either series of CDK8/19 inhibitors, or other chemotypes with similar profiles, would be extremely challenging based on the complex toxicological profile and an inability to define a clear therapeutic window.
source: These observations indicate that the clinical development of either series of CDK8/19 inhibitors, or other chemotypes with similar profiles, would be extremely challenging.
evidence: The claim is presented as a conclusion based on the toxicological findings.

claim: A recent study with the natural product CDK8/19 inhibitor cortistatin A found a treatment-induced gene expression profile distinct from the profile resulting from CDK8/19 shRNA knockouts in the same cell line.
source: The potential difference between loss of protein and inhibition of enzymatic activity is highlighted by a recent study with the natural product CDK8/19 inhibitor cortistatin A that found a treatment-induced gene expression profile distinct from the profile resulting from CDK8/19 shRNA knockouts in the same cell line (Poss et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Poss et al., 2016).

claim: Despite reproducible inhibition of TCF/LEF reporter activity and STAT1SER727 phosphorylation by both series of compounds, only modest, though generally significant, antiproliferative or antitumor effects were detected in vitro or in vivo.
source: Despite reproducible inhibition of TCF/LEF reporter activity and STAT1SER727 phosphorylation by both series of compounds, we were only able to detect modest, though generally significant, antiproliferative or antitumor effects in vitro or in vivo.
evidence: The claim is presented as a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: Compounds from the 3,4,5-trisubstituted pyridine series had only modest effects in vitro and little effect in vivo on PDX tumors despite maximal inhibition of STAT1SER727 phosphorylation.
source: In follow-up studies on cell cultures derived from PDX tumors, and selected PDXs in vivo, we found that compounds from the 3,4,5-trisubstituted pyridine series had only modest effects in vitro and little effect in vivo despite maximal inhibition of STAT1SER727 phosphorylation.
evidence: The claim is presented as a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: Both series of compounds showed greater potency in a systemic or subcutaneous model of human AML, similar to that reported for the natural product inhibitor of CDK8/19, cortistatin A.
source: The pleiotropic nature of CDK8/19 function, influencing the activity of multiple specific transcription factors and also super-enhancers, may make identification of biomarkers for particular cancer cell types that are especially sensitive to CDK8/19 inhibitors challenging; despite this both series of compounds did show greater potency in a systemic or subcutaneous model of human AML, similar to that reported for the natural product inhibitor of CDK8/19, cortistatin A (Pelish et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Pelish et al., 2015) and the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The in vivo activity of the CDK8/19 inhibitory compounds was associated with modulation of gene expression regulated by transcription factors that are CDK8 substrates.
source: We found that the in vivo activity of our CDK8/19 inhibitory compounds was associated with modulation of gene expression regulated by transcription factors that are CDK8 substrates.
evidence: The claim is presented as a summary of the gene expression profiling findings.

source: Moreover, Pelish and colleagues (Pelish et al., 2015) recently demonstrated that in AML cells CDK8 is associated with gene super-enhancers and that pharmacological inhibition of CDK8 activated super-enhancer output.

source: Here, we also found that pharmacological inhibition of CDK8 with our potent and selective chemical probes in colorectal cancer models resulted in gene expression profiles consistent with increased super-enhancer activity.
evidence: The claim is presented as a summary of the gene expression profiling findings.

claim: CDK8 activity maintains embryonic stem cells in an undifferentiated, pluripotent state and colorectal tumors in a de-differentiated state.
source: CDK8 activity maintains embryonic stem cells in an undifferentiated, pluripotent state and colorectal tumors in a de-differentiated state (Adler et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Adler et al., 2012).

claim: Complete inhibition of CDK8/19 in the presence of activated oncogenic beta-catenin mimicked the effect of reducing, rather than completely abrogating, WNT-signaling.
source: We found that complete inhibition of CDK8/19 in the presence of activated oncogenic beta-catenin mimicked the effect of reducing, rather than completely abrogating, WNT-signaling.
evidence: The claim is presented as a summary of the experimental findings in the beta-catenin mouse model.

claim: CDK8/19 inhibition resulted in a shift from a stem cell to a predominantly TA cell phenotype in the beta-catenin mouse model.
source: CDK8/19 inhibition resulted in a shift from a stem cell to a predominantly TA cell phenotype.
evidence: The claim is presented as a summary of the experimental findings in the beta-catenin mouse model.

source: This response may also be linked to super-enhancer activation, as expression of Myc, a super-enhancer-regulated gene (Lovén et al., 2013), was repressed in the stem cell population, but elevated in the TA cell population following compound treatment.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Lovén et al., 2013) and the experimental data.

claim: Myc is a super-enhancer-regulated gene.

evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Lovén et al., 2013).

claim: Cellular context will have a major impact on the transcriptional response to CDK8 inhibition.
source: The example of Myc illustrates the potential complexity of the response to CDK8 inhibition, as Myc expression will potentially be repressed through loss of CDK8 activity required by beta-catenin, but Myc expression may also be promoted through super-enhancer activation. This suggests that cellular context will have a major impact on the transcriptional response to CDK8 inhibition.
evidence: The claim is presented as a conclusion based on the observation of context-dependent effects on Myc expression.

claim: Compounds 3 and 4 produced unusually extensive, but similar, adverse effects in a wide range of tissues in rat and dog tolerability studies.
source: In rat and dog tolerability studies, we found that 3 and 4 produced unusually extensive, but similar, adverse effects in a wide range of tissues.
evidence: The claim is presented as a summary of the tolerability study findings.

claim: The breadth, degree and depth of adverse effects of CDK8/19 inhibition is perhaps not surprising given the reported role of CDK8 in repressing super-enhancer activity and the potentially key roles of super-enhancers as master controllers of cell identity and function.
source: Given our observations, that are consistent with the reported role of CDK8 in repressing super-enhancer activity (Pelish et al., 2015), and the potentially key roles of super-enhancers as master controllers of cell identity and function (Whyte et al., 2013), the breadth, degree and depth of adverse effects is perhaps not surprising.
evidence: The claim is presented as a speculation based on the known roles of CDK8 and super-enhancers, supported by citations to published literature (Pelish et al., 2015; Whyte et al., 2013).

claim: Elevated IL-12 in rats treated with compound 3 may result from decreased STAT1SER727 following CDK8 inhibition, as bone marrow macrophages from STAT1S727A mutant mice exhibit elevated IL-12 and Cox-2 expression following activation.
source: We detected elevation of the mainly proinflammatory and proimmunestimulatory associated cytokine, IL-12, in rats treated with 3. evidence: The claim is presented as a speculation based on the experimental observation and supported by a citation to published literature (Schroder et al., 2007).

claim: Cox-2 induction is associated with an increased production of PGE2, which was detected in vitro.
source: Cox-2 induction is associated with an increased production of PGE2, which we detected in vitro, that may also explain the unusual split response of increased IL-17A and decreased IL-17F observed in our in vitro experiments, since PGE2, or agonists of the EP receptor for PGE2 are among the few stimuli that induce this split effect (Melton et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data and a citation to published literature (Melton et al., 2013).

claim: PGE2, or agonists of the EP receptor for PGE2 are among the few stimuli that induce the split effect of increased IL-17A and decreased IL-17F.
