evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Melton et al., 2013).

claim: The multiplicity of preclinical pathomorphological lesions would make monitoring and controlling toxicity in a clinical study very challenging.
source: We concluded that the multiplicity of preclinical pathomorphological lesions would make monitoring and controlling toxicity in a clinical study very challenging, especially as no clear safety window could be established from our studies.
evidence: The claim is presented as a conclusion based on the toxicological findings.

claim: The adverse effects of CDK8/19 inhibition are target related as they are detected with two chemically distinct series of potent and selective CDK8/19 ligands.
source: Our data strongly suggest that the adverse effects are target related as they are detected with two chemically distinct series of potent and selective CDK8/19 ligands and indicate that dual pharmacological CDK8/19 inhibition is not tolerated in rats or dogs at exposure levels that correspond to therapeutically relevant exposures.
evidence: The claim is presented as a conclusion based on the observation of similar adverse effects with two structurally distinct inhibitors.

claim: Dual pharmacological CDK8/19 inhibition is not tolerated in rats or dogs at exposure levels that correspond to therapeutically relevant exposures.
source: Our data strongly suggest that the adverse effects are target related as they are detected with two chemically distinct series of potent and selective CDK8/19 ligands and indicate that dual pharmacological CDK8/19 inhibition is not tolerated in rats or dogs at exposure levels that correspond to therapeutically relevant exposures.
evidence: The claim is presented as a conclusion based on the toxicological findings.

claim: Even in the more sensitive xenograft models of AML, there was no clear therapeutic window, as these tumors responded only when STAT1SER727 phosphorylation was continuously inhibited and equivalent exposures were not tolerated in in vivo rat and dog toleration studies.
source: Even in the more sensitive xenograft models of AML, there was no clear therapeutic window, as these tumors responded only when STAT1SER727 phosphorylation was continuously inhibited and equivalent exposures were not tolerated in our in vivo rat and dog toleration studies.
evidence: The claim is presented as a conclusion based on the comparison of efficacy and tolerability data.

claim: CDK8/19 are identified as potential 'anti-targets' to be avoided in drug discovery.
source: Our observations are important for both scenarios as we identify CDK8/19 as potential 'anti-targets' to be avoided and we recommend screening against these protein kinases when establishing the safety profile of lead compounds and development candidates as well as assessing the quality of chemical probes.
evidence: The claim is presented as a recommendation based on the toxicological findings.

claim: Screening against CDK8/19 is recommended when establishing the safety profile of lead compounds and development candidates as well as assessing the quality of chemical probes.
source: Our observations are important for both scenarios as we identify CDK8/19 as potential 'anti-targets' to be avoided and we recommend screening against these protein kinases when establishing the safety profile of lead compounds and development candidates as well as assessing the quality of chemical probes.
evidence: The claim is presented as a recommendation based on the toxicological findings.

claim: Cortistatin A was recently reported as a CDK8/19 inhibitor with specificity, potency, favourable pharmacokinetics that would make it a useful in vitro and in vivo probe for the Mediator kinases and as a promising lead for development of therapeutics.
source: As described earlier, the natural product cortistatin A was recently reported by Pelish and colleagues as a CDK8/19 inhibitor with specificity, potency, favourable pharmacokinetics that would make it a useful in vitro and in vivo probe for the Mediator kinases and as a promising lead for development of therapeutics (Pelish et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Pelish et al., 2015).

claim: The synthetic compounds (3 and 4) are much less challenging to synthesise compared to cortistatin A.
source: Here, we employed two different series of potent and selective CDK8/19 inhibitors, with paired negative controls, that are much less challenging to synthesise compared to cortistatin A (Pelish et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is presented as a comparison with cortistatin A, supported by a citation to published literature (Pelish et al., 2015).

claim: The synthetic compounds (3 and 4) have optimal pharmacological and pharmaceutical properties with single digit nM affinities for CDK8/19 and low nanomolar activity against promoter and STAT1SER727 reporter assays and are as potent as cortistatin A.
source: Our synthetic compounds have optimal pharmacological and pharmaceutical properties with single digit nM affinities for CDK8/19 and low nanomolar activity against promoter and STAT1SER727 reporter assays and are as potent as cortistatin A, as well as exhibiting very high selectivity in broad kinome profiling.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The synthetic compounds (3 and 4) exhibit very high selectivity in broad kinome profiling.
source: Our synthetic compounds have optimal pharmacological and pharmaceutical properties with single digit nM affinities for CDK8/19 and low nanomolar activity against promoter and STAT1SER727 reporter assays and are as potent as cortistatin A, as well as exhibiting very high selectivity in broad kinome profiling.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Similar induction of super-enhancer-regulated genes was found with the synthetic compounds as described by Pelish and colleagues for cortistatin A, although the profiling was done in tumours treated in vivo rather than in vitro.
source: As described by Pelish and colleagues for cortistatin A, we found similar induction of super-enhancer-regulated genes with our compounds, although note that in our case we profiled gene expression in tumours treated in vivo rather than in vitro (Pelish et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Pelish et al., 2015) and the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Similar to cortistatin A, the synthetic compounds were tolerated in mice and AMLs were found to be highly sensitive in vivo models.
source: Similar to cortistatin A our compounds were also tolerated in mice and likewise we also found AMLs to be highly sensitive in vivo models (Pelish et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Pelish et al., 2015) and the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The detailed toxicity profile of cortistatin A was not reported by Pelish and colleagues.
source: However, in our study we also evaluated our two series in dedicated tolerability studies in rat and dog that revealed toxicity not apparent in mouse studies. The detailed toxicity profile of cortistatin A was not reported by Pelish and colleagues, but given the similarities in the results from in vitro and in vivo studies between cortistatin A and our two series we predict that cortistatin A and other CDK8/19 inhibitors would exhibit similar toxicity.
evidence: The claim is based on the absence of detailed toxicity information in the cited publication.

claim: Given the similarities in the results from in vitro and in vivo studies between cortistatin A and the two synthetic series, it is predicted that cortistatin A and other CDK8/19 inhibitors would exhibit similar toxicity.
source: However, in our study we also evaluated our two series in dedicated tolerability studies in rat and dog that revealed toxicity not apparent in mouse studies. The detailed toxicity profile of cortistatin A was not reported by Pelish and colleagues, but given the similarities in the results from in vitro and in vivo studies between cortistatin A and our two series we predict that cortistatin A and other CDK8/19 inhibitors would exhibit similar toxicity.
evidence: The claim is presented as a prediction based on the similarities in efficacy and mechanism of action.

claim: CDK8/19 inhibitors might modulate antitumor immunotherapy by inactivating STAT1 and stimulating tumor surveillance by NK cells.
source: It remains to be seen if toxicity could be avoided if CDK8/19 inhibitors were administered intermittently as part of a combination therapy. For example, CDK8/19 inhibitors might modulate antitumor immunotherapy by inactivating STAT1 and stimulating tumor surveillance by NK cells (Putz et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is presented as a speculation supported by a citation to published literature (Putz et al., 2013).

claim: During the optimisation of both the 3,4,5-trisubstituted pyridine and 3-methyl-1H-pyrazolo[3,4-b]pyridine series, the authors were unable to separate CDK8 from CDK19 affinity.
source: It is also unclear if toxicity could be avoided by selectively targeting CDK8 or CDK19 alone. During the optimisation of both the 3,4,5-trisubstituted pyridine and 3-methyl-1H-pyrazolo[3,4-b]pyridine series, we were unable to separate CDK8 from CDK19 affinity (Mallinger et al., 2015, 2016a; Czodrowski et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to the authors' previous publications (Mallinger et al., 2015, 2016a; Czodrowski et al., 2016).

claim: Two additional distinct chemical series identified by the authors and three chemotypes from the literature all demonstrated balanced CDK8 and CDK19 affinity.
source: This is also true for two additional distinct chemical series that we identified (Schiemann et al., 2016; Mallinger et al., 2016b), and also for a further three chemotypes we profiled from the literature, all of which demonstrated balanced CDK8 and CDK19 affinity in our hands.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to the authors' previous publications (Schiemann et al., 2016; Mallinger et al., 2016b).

claim: The natural product cortistatin A cannot selectively distinguish between CDK8 and 19.
source: Similarly, the natural product cortistatin A cannot selectively distinguish between CDK8 and 19 (Pelish et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Pelish et al., 2015).

claim: The inability to selectively target CDK8 or CDK19 is likely due to the very high degree of sequence similarity around the active site of these two kinases.
source: The inability to selectively target CDK8 or CDK19 is likely due to the very high degree of sequence similarity around the active site of these two kinases (Figure 1c), suggesting that strategies to selectively target either of these paralogs will require a different approach, such as allosteric modulation or selective degradation.
evidence: The claim is presented as an inference based on the sequence similarity shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Strategies to selectively target either CDK8 or CDK19 will require a different approach, such as allosteric modulation or selective degradation.
source: The inability to selectively target CDK8 or CDK19 is likely due to the very high degree of sequence similarity around the active site of these two kinases (Figure 1c), suggesting that strategies to selectively target either of these paralogs will require a different approach, such as allosteric modulation or selective degradation.
evidence: The claim is presented as a speculation based on the inability to achieve selectivity with ATP-competitive inhibitors.

claim: Selective inhibitors of the transcriptional kinases CDK7 or CDK12/13 have been recently identified.
source: The recent identification of selective inhibitors of the transcriptional kinases CDK7 or CDK12/13 has fuelled interest in the clinical development of inhibitors of these targets (Kwiatkowski et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2016; Christensen et al., 2014; Chipumuro et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Kwiatkowski et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2016; Christensen et al., 2014; Chipumuro et al., 2014).

source: This is of relevance here as inhibition of these kinases has also been reported to affect super-enhancer-associated gene expression in T cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, B cell chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, MYCN-driven tumours, small cell lung cancer and triple negative breast cancer models where anti-tumour activity is observed (Kwiatkowski et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2016; Christensen et al., 2014; Chipumuro et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Kwiatkowski et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2016; Christensen et al., 2014; Chipumuro et al., 2014).

source: In adult CDK7 conditional knockout mice, effects were seen in tissues with a high cell turnover that were at least in part due to a depleted stem cell population resulting from a loss of CDK1 and CDK2 activation or reduced super-enhancer-associated gene expression (Ganuza et al., 2012).

source: Super-enhancers are frequently found associated with genes whose products control the pluripotent state or define cell identity and this may make stem cell populations particularly vulnerable to therapeutic interventions that interfere with super-enhancer associated gene expression, including inhibitors of the transcription-regulating CDKs (Whyte et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is presented as a speculation based on the role of super-enhancers in stem cell function, supported by a citation to published literature (Whyte et al., 2013).

claim: CDK8/19 inhibitors altered the proportion of stem cells to proliferative TA cells in an in vivo mouse model of an oncogenically-activated stem cell compartment, which may in part be due to super-enhancer activation.
source: In an in vivo mouse model of an oncogenically-activated stem cell compartment we found our CDK8/19 inhibitors altered the proportion of stem cells to proliferative TA cells that may in part be due to super-enhancer activation.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The stem cell compartment may require a precise 'dosage' of super-enhancer activity and that activation or inhibition of super-enhancer activity will negatively impact the stem cell compartment.
source: This raises the hypothetical possibility that, similar to AML cells (Pelish et al., 2015), the stem cell compartment requires a precise 'dosage' of super-enhancer activity and that activation or inhibition of super-enhancer activity will negatively impact the stem cell compartment.
evidence: The claim is presented as a speculation based on the experimental observations and comparison to AML cells, supported by a citation to published literature (Pelish et al., 2015).

claim: The selective CDK7 tool inhibitors are reported to be tolerated in mice and so predicted to be non-toxic.
source: The selective CDK7 tool inhibitors are reported to be tolerated in mice and so predicted to be non-toxic (Kwiatkowski et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2015; Christensen et al., 2014; Chipumuro et al., 2014); however, our CDK8/19 inhibitors were also tolerated in mice and the toxicity was not revealed until detailed tolerability studies were performed in other species.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Kwiatkowski et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2015; Christensen et al., 2014; Chipumuro et al., 2014).

claim: The true toxicity profile of other transcriptional CDK inhibitors may not be revealed until dedicated tolerability studies are performed using selective compounds with optimised pharmaceutical properties.
source: The selective CDK7 tool inhibitors are reported to be tolerated in mice and so predicted to be non-toxic (Kwiatkowski et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2015; Christensen et al., 2014; Chipumuro et al., 2014); however, our CDK8/19 inhibitors were also tolerated in mice and the toxicity was not revealed until detailed tolerability studies were performed in other species. Thus the true toxicity profile of other transcriptional CDK inhibitors may not be revealed until dedicated tolerability studies are performed using selective compounds with optimised pharmaceutical properties.
evidence: The claim is presented as a conclusion based on the comparison of the authors' findings with CDK8/19 inhibitors to the reported tolerability of CDK7 inhibitors.

claim: The authors have decided against the further clinical development of their CDK8/19 inhibitor compounds based on the complex toxicological profile and an inability to define a clear therapeutic window.
source: However, on the basis of the complex toxicological profile and an inability to define a clear therapeutic window, we have decided against the further clinical development of our compounds and suggest caution when considering the clinical applicability of other CDK8/19 inhibitors.
evidence: The claim is presented as a decision based on the toxicological findings.

claim: The authors suggest caution when considering the clinical applicability of other CDK8/19 inhibitors.
